extracted.intended_audience: visitors and sportsmen who follow or wish to follow fell foxhounds in the Lake District (Lakeland)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and standards for participating in foxhunting on the Lakeland fells: equipment, clothing, navigation, safety, and reading the ground and scenting conditions. Focused on what a follower must do or expect to take part safely and effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Travel on foot (horses impracticable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Except in some portions of the low ground, riding to hounds is impossible; the man who would see something of the work of the mountain hounds must be prepared to face the hills on Shanks’s pony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect to ride to hounds on the high fells; plan to walk the routes, follow local hunters' lead, and use walking routes that gain the tops. On low ground, side-roads and bridle-tracks may allow mounted followers to keep touch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical fitness and conditioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless heart and lungs are sound, and one is in some kind of training, fell climbing is astonishingly hard work, and becomes much more of a toil than a pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared for very early rises, long days, steep climbs, scrambling over scree and crags; train cardio and legs before attempting sustained fell hunting days.

rubrics_metrics.name: Footwear: stout, well-nailed boots; avoid thin shoes
rubrics_metrics.description: Thin boots or shoes, with smooth soles, are useless as well as dangerous. What is required is a good stout shooting boot, well nailed to prevent slipping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use anklets to stop grit entering boot tops; avoid shoes that give no ankle support. Proper soles and nails reduce slipping on steep, scree-strewn or icy ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clothing: thick, wet-resisting; prefer loose knickerbockers
rubrics_metrics.description: The clothing should be fairly thick and wet-resisting. Loose knickerbockers are better than knicker-breeches, as the latter restrain the free action of the knees and make climbing harder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dress for cold, wind and wet conditions at altitude; expect hoarfrost, driving rain and snow even when lowlands are mild.

rubrics_metrics.name: Walking-stick choice
rubrics_metrics.description: A stick of some kind is a great help, but I do not recommend the long, alpenstock affairs sold to summer visitors. An ordinary stout walking-stick is the best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid long sticks that trip you on steep ground; a stout walking-stick offers support without creating a hazard on descents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stay on the tops unless hounds are viewing the fox
rubrics_metrics.description: Having once reached the tops, it is wise to stay at that altitude, unless hounds are practically viewing their fox, and driving him hard towards the dale. It is much quicker to go round the tops than to make a descent to the dale and then climb out again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan routes that keep you on the ridge/top; descending and re-climbing wastes time and energy and risks missing the hunt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Navigation and mist safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Mist is the greatest bugbear of the fell foxhunter — once the tops are shrouded there is nothing but the cry of hounds to direct you, and it is surprisingly easy to lose direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If lost or in impenetrable mist, get below the mist to discover your whereabouts; use landmarks (peat hags, cairns, watercourses) to orientate; avoid blind descents in mist. Be aware that sound is deceptive on the fells (echoes/misdirection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weather hazards: snow, ice and wind
rubrics_metrics.description: At altitude snow can be deep and frost severe. Snowstorms seldom stop hunting, but frozen snow and iciness on crags make terrain unsafe. Driving wind can obliterate all sounds and physically lift light objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize when hunting should be abandoned for safety (frozen crags, dangerous ice). Expect wind to mask hounds and to make travel arduous; plan for hoarfrost and extreme cold at altitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dangerous crags and known accident spots
rubrics_metrics.description: Many of the huge crags on the fells are dangerous for hounds and followers; several named crags have been scenes of accidents and rescues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn local hazardous features (e.g., Goat’s Water, Pavey Ark, Dove Crag, Raven Crag) and keep clear of overhanging or icy ledges. Exercise caution when approaching crag edges and steep drops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand bracken’s effect on scent and ground visitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Bracken is waist-high in summer and hampers footsteps; because of its dryness, it makes scenting conditions very difficult. For this reason hounds seldom visit the low ground until a fall of snow or heavy rain has somewhat flattened the bracken beds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect low-ground sport to improve only after rain or snow flattens bracken; anticipate poor scenting in tall bracken patches and adjust where you position yourself accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and prefer 'good running ground'
rubrics_metrics.description: High-fell tracts of fairly level, short, thick turf are known as 'good running ground' where on a decent scenting day hounds can press their fox severely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing where to follow, seek these fairly level summit tracts for the best chance to see hounds work and run; steep, craggy ground limits hunting visibility and hounds’ pace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scent unpredictability
rubrics_metrics.description: Scent is variable; often very good in damp snow, but at times the reverse. 'There’s nowt sae queer as scent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume consistent scenting conditions; plan for rapid changes and recognize that weather/time-of-day (drying dew) affect scent early in autumn and spring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of vehicles and bicycles on low ground
rubrics_metrics.description: A car, a motor cycle, or even the humble 'push-bike' are extremely useful at times during the course of a run with the fell hounds to slip along in touch with hounds on low ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cycles/cars strategically (leave a cycle where it may be needed) to keep touch on stretches where roads run parallel to the hunt; on open fells these are less useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: If injured or incapacitated, seek help or wait for daylight
rubrics_metrics.description: A sprained ankle can place a man in a very awkward position; if alone and injured one might have to pass a night on the open fell. If night is drawing on, it is better to wait for daylight than risk breaking a leg or your neck over some crag.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize staying put and conserving warmth if injured; seek fellow hunters or find roads/inhabitated places when possible; carry means of signalling or basic first aid where practicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid risky descents at night
rubrics_metrics.description: On a dark night, striking matches or peering about in rough ground is thankless. With a moon and clear sky you may be safe enough, but generally do not risk a descent in the dark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan route timing to avoid being on remote tops after dusk; if caught, wait for dawn rather than risk hazardous navigation or falls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of snow-blindness and eye protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflected light from crusted snow can be intense and may lead to snow-blindness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wear appropriate eye protection (sunglasses/goggles) or avoid prolonged exposure to intense reflected glare; move to less glaring positions if symptoms occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know local fox habits and likely kennels
rubrics_metrics.description: Fell foxes often make their kennels on 'benks' (ledges) sheltered from wind with a wide view; lower coverts and larch plantations may hold foxes but the fell fox prefers higher altitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When positioning yourself to view or intercept, consider sheltered ledges and benks above the lower slopes as likely fox lairs; study local topography to anticipate where a fox may bolt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan for provisions and endurance (long day requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: A day’s hunting is always something of a lottery and may involve a very early rise, a long day in the open air, steep climbs, long waits, and exposure to the elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carry food ('a “piece” in your pocket'), suitable drink, and prepare mentally/physically for long hours; low subscription rates mean little else is required financially but endurance and preparation are essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local customs after a kill
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the custom in Lakeland to take the carcass of the fox to the nearest inn, where it is hung from a 'crook' in the ceiling of the bar-parlour, for all to see.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of and respect local hunting traditions and etiquette following a kill; this is part of the social fabric of fell hunting.
